scenes.heading: Genetic engineering
scenes.sub: How do bacteria end up making human insulin?
scenes.say: Genetic engineering is changing an organism's DNA in the lab, usually by adding a gene from another organism. It's how bacteria can make human insulin for people with diabetes.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Copy a paragraph and paste it into another document
scenes.science: Cut a gene out and paste it into another organism's DNA
scenes.breaks: on a computer you can cut anywhere; a restriction enzyme only cuts where its specific base sequence appears.
scenes.say: It's like copy and paste. A pasted paragraph still makes sense because both documents use the same alphabet. All living things use the same DNA code, so a human gene pasted into a bacterium can still be read.

scenes.heading: Cut, paste, deliver
points: They cut at recognition sites, leaving sticky ends
scenes.say: Restriction enzymes are the scissors. They cut DNA at specific recognition sites, often leaving sticky ends. DNA ligase is the glue that seals pieces together. And a plasmid, a small circle of bacterial DNA, is the vector that carries the gene in.

scenes.heading: Same scissors, matching pieces
points: on the gene and the plasmid
Sticky ends pair: A with T, C with G
Ligase seals the backbone for good
scenes.say: Use the same restriction enzyme on the gene and the plasmid, so their sticky ends fit like matching puzzle pieces. The bases pair up, A with T and C with G. Those bonds are weak, so ligase seals the backbone for good.

scenes.heading: Making human insulin
steps: Cut gene and plasmid with same enzyme
Put into bacteria; use a marker gene
Grow in tanks; purify the insulin
scenes.say: To make insulin, identify the human insulin gene. Cut it and a plasmid with the same enzyme, and join them with ligase. Put the recombinant plasmids into bacteria, and use a marker gene to find the ones that took them up. Grow them in big tanks and purify the insulin.

scenes.heading: GM crops: benefits and risks
scenes.say: Genes can be added to crops too, like Bt cotton grown in Australia, which makes a protein toxic to certain insect pests. Benefits include fewer sprays and better nutrition. Risks include genes spreading to wild plants and pests evolving resistance.

scenes.heading: Bt cotton
scenes.question: A farmer grows Bt cotton for years and sprays less. Later, more pests survive on the crop. Why?
lines: A few pests already had a resistance mutation
Bt toxin killed most non-resistant pests
Refuges of non-Bt crops slow this
scenes.say: Why do more pests survive Bt cotton after a few years? A few already had a resistance mutation. The toxin killed the rest, so resistant pests bred and became more common. That's natural selection, and refuges of non-Bt crops slow it down.

points: All life uses the same DNA code
GM crops have benefits and risks
scenes.say: Quick recap. Genetic engineering works because all life shares one DNA code. Restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins, and plasmids deliver. Now try the practice questions!
